clue.text: Crowd of millions on Belarus's western borders

indicators.note: on a map west is the left-hand side, so the western border of each word is its leftmost letter

parts.note: first letter of millions
first letter of on
first letter of Belarus

explanation.surface: A news report of a huge crowd massing at the western frontier of Belarus.
explanation.walkthrough: Belarus looks like the star of the clue, but it only supplies its first letter; 'western borders' reads as geography and means the left-hand edge of each word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names a large, unruly throng of people, usually an angry one.

clue.text: Pulp hit needs no introduction

indicators.note: the introduction of a word is its opening letter, and this word does without it

parts.note: a smash hit is a big success

explanation.surface: A pop smash so famous that nobody needs to introduce it, perhaps a pulp fiction bestseller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needs no introduction' is a showbiz cliché, but here it is literal: the word for hit loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: As verbs both mean crushing food or other soft material into a soft, shapeless paste.

clue.text: Licensed premises above Top Man in East London town

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece is written physically above the second

parts.note: a place licensed to sell alcohol
the man at the very top of a kingdom

explanation.surface: A pub sitting over a Top Man clothes shop on an East London high street.
explanation.walkthrough: Top Man is a British high-street menswear chain, which makes the shop-above-the-pub picture plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Barking is a district in the London borough of Barking and Dagenham, east of the City.

clue.text: I'd put back vegetable juice before vegetable wine went

indicators.note: to put a word back is to set it running backwards
the pieces so far come ahead of the final one, the wine

parts.note: I'D, apostrophe dropped, before turning round
the juice of a plant
a green vegetable in a pod
red wine, as ordered at a bar

explanation.surface: A home cook blending vegetable juice and then finding the wine had vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vegetable' appears twice and does two different jobs: first as part of 'vegetable juice', then alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: something that vanished from sight went away.

clue.text: Done up smartly, Ant's best man made a speech

parts.note: Ant and Dec are a British TV presenting duo; Ant's partner
to orate is to speechify

explanation.surface: At a wedding, the best man in his finery stands up to give his speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant and Dec are a hugely famous British TV double act, so 'Ant's best man' is his partner, not a wedding role.
explanation.definitionFit: A room or tree trimmed with ornaments has been decked out, made to look smart and festive.

clue.text: Get to hear the first part of Carmen

indicators.note: to hear means the letter is said aloud and a word sounding like it is entered

parts.note: the opera title Carmen begins with the letter C, said aloud here

explanation.surface: An invitation to go and listen to the opening of Bizet's opera Carmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the first part of' Carmen is the letter C, which said 'to hear' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To get something, in the sense of understanding it, is to see it: 'I see' means 'I understand'.

clue.text: Voucher from a posh dude accepted by Bill

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so these pieces go inside the last one

parts.note: a bill is a poster, as in 'stick no bills'; it splits POST…ER round the rest
a titled toff
a as printed

explanation.surface: A voucher handed over by a toff and accepted by someone called Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name but is a notice pasted on a wall. A postal order is a British money order bought at a post office.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper slip bought at a post office and cashed by the payee, so a kind of money voucher.

clue.text: Striking effect of knitted lace on Twiggy's top

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above, so the anagram comes before the next letter
knitted yarn is looped and interwoven, so the letters of lace are worked into a new order
top points to the opening letter of the word Twiggy's

parts.note: the 1960s model, here only supplying her first letter

explanation.surface: A fashion note: Twiggy's knitted lace top makes a striking impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knitted' rearranges LACE as ECLA, which sits 'on' T, the 'top' of Twiggy's. Twiggy was a famous British model of the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: The French borrowing means brilliance or a dazzling display, a striking show of success.

clue.text: The start of Emmanuel Macron's unconventional love affair

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
unconventional means not in the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: first letter of Emmanuel
the surname as printed

explanation.surface: A remark on the French president's famously unusual marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface alludes to Emmanuel Macron's marriage to his former teacher, and the answer's letters are almost all in his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a romantic relationship between two people, often a brief or secret one.

clue.text: District attorney starts to reflect and knowingly question something hitherto unperceived

indicators.note: the starts of the words that follow are their first letters

parts.note: the standard US abbreviation
first letter of reflect
first letter of knowingly
an issue, as in 'a matter of taste'

explanation.surface: A prosecutor pausing to think and pointedly ask about something no one had noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' sits between the two words whose first letters are taken, so only 'reflect' and 'knowingly' contribute.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronomers infer this invisible mass from gravity but have never directly detected it, hence unperceived.

clue.text: Sons followed by exhausted parents with salad stuck in teeth

indicators.note: followed by places the abbreviation for sons ahead of what comes next

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son or sons

indicators.note: stuck in means jammed inside, so the salad leaf goes between those outer letters
exhausted means emptied, so only the outside letters of parents remain

parts.note: the word whose outer letters are kept
rocket is a peppery salad leaf, also called arugula

explanation.surface: Weary parents, followed by their sons, find bits of salad caught in their teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exhausted' empties PARENTS to PS, and ROCKET is 'stuck in' it, all after S. The definition is the clue's last word, though the surface treats teeth as a human mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The cogs on a bicycle's chain wheel are toothed projections, so teeth stands for the answer.

clue.text: Madagascan ruler not the first to regret misguidely taking money

indicators.note: the first letter of regret is R, and the ruler goes without it
the rearranged letters take in one more piece
misguided letters go astray and end up in a new order

parts.words: ruler not the first to regret
parts.note: RULER without an R, the first letter of regret
m = money, as in £5m

explanation.surface: A ruler of Madagascar who, unlike others, regrets foolishly taking bribes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madagascan ruler' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Madagascan' used as a noun; the blog notes RULER has two Rs and only one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by origin: these primates live wild only on the island of Madagascar, so one is a Madagascan native.

clue.text: Newspaper that prompts self-reflection

definitions.meaning: reflection taken literally: the glass that shows you your own face

explanation.surface: A paper whose articles make readers think about themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-reflection' reads as soul-searching but is meant literally, your own image in the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: The Daily Mirror is a long-running British tabloid, and a looking glass throws back your own image.

clue.text: State in which The Departed is set

definitions.text: State in which The Departed is set

parts.words: State in which The Departed is set
parts.note: the surface reading: which US state is Scorsese's film The Departed set in?; the setter's reading: the departed are the dead, and 'set' means stiffened; the state is a bodily condition

explanation.surface: A film-trivia question about where Scorsese's The Departed takes place.
explanation.walkthrough: The Departed is a Scorsese film set in Boston, Massachusetts, so 'state' suggests a US state; read literally, the departed are the dead and 'set' means stiffened.
explanation.definitionFit: After death the muscles stiffen for a time, so a corpse is set rigid in this condition.

clue.text: Distant relative to close cycling function on the outskirts of Yarm

indicators.note: cycling moves the end letter of the word round to its front

parts.note: tan is the trigonometric function tangent
taken as written

indicators.note: the outskirts are the edges, so the first and last letters of Yarm are used

parts.note: a market town in North Yorkshire, England

explanation.surface: A distant relative, living on the edge of the town of Yarm, cycles in to a family function.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' turns TAN into ANT, then ON, then YM from 'the outskirts of' Yarm. The definition is cryptic: distant is this to close.
explanation.definitionFit: Distant and close are opposites, so distant stands in relation to close as a word of opposite meaning.

clue.text: Olympic sport during which tension makes people jumpy

definitions.text: Olympic sport during which tension makes people jumpy

parts.words: Olympic sport during which tension makes people jumpy
parts.note: the surface reading: nerves before a big final leave the competitors on edge; the setter's reading: the tension is in a taut sprung bed, and the people really do jump

explanation.surface: An Olympic event so nerve-racking it leaves competitors on edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tension' and 'jumpy' read as nerves; here the tension is in springs and fabric, and the athletes literally bounce.
explanation.definitionFit: Gymnasts bounce on a taut sprung bed in this event, which has been part of the Olympics since 2000.

clue.text: Fair, intelligent leader gets kicked out

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and it is expelled

parts.note: clever

explanation.surface: A just and clever political leader is ousted anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: The political leader of the surface is simply the leading letter of the word for intelligent.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fair decision is a just one, correct and proper.

clue.text: Dopiest tigers go swimming around midnight

indicators.note: letters that go swimming drift about into a new order
the rearranged letters wrap around another piece
the middle of the word night is its central letter

parts.note: anagram fodder
the middle letter of NIGHT

explanation.surface: Sleepy tigers taking a dip in the middle of the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' belongs to the fodder, not to the instruction, and 'midnight' is the middle of the word night, a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlatives of dazed and sluggish: the most dopey person is the one most befuddled, as after sleep or drink.

clue.text: Test participant flipping second of two coins ahead of game's opening

indicators.note: the two coins come ahead of, in front of, the letter that follows in the answer

parts.note: the first of the two coins: a guinea, the old British gold coin worth 21 shillings

indicators.note: only the second of the two coins is flipped over, so that coin alone is read backwards

parts.note: the second of the two coins: 1P, a one-penny piece, written as letters

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, taken from the word that precedes it

parts.note: first letter of game

explanation.surface: A volunteer in a trial tossing a coin before the match kicks off.
explanation.walkthrough: The coins are GUINEA and 1P (one penny, written IP); 'flipping second of' turns only the penny round, giving PI; these go 'ahead of' G, the 'opening' of 'game's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic: the pet rodent was long used in laboratory experiments, so its name passed to any person being tested on.

clue.text: Twisted title of Prince Philip's matrimonial memoirs? English Duke

parts.words: title of Prince Philip's matrimonial memoirs?
parts.note: 'Me and ER': Philip and his wife, ER being Elizabeth Regina
e = English
d = Duke

explanation.surface: An imagined book title for the Duke of Edinburgh's memoirs of his marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen; the question mark flags an invented title.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of wandering in bends: a river or road that wound about in curves twisted along its way.

clue.text: Like 19 or 20

parts.note: as = like, as in 'dressed as a pirate'
the number read as its digits 1 and 9: Roman I, then the nine spelt out

explanation.walkthrough: '19' looks like a pointer to this very clue, but it is read as its digits; '20' does point to another answer, 20 across, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The 20 across answer means silly, and this word, literally like a donkey, means stupid in just that way.

clue.text: Silly old lady that is seen about

indicators.note: 'that is' is seen standing about, around, the old lady

parts.note: i.e. = id est, that is; it goes round the old lady
nan = grandmother, in British speech

explanation.surface: A daft old woman spotted out and about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is a British word for grandmother, and the abbreviation for 'that is' wraps round her.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe remarks or behaviour that are pointless and lacking sense.

clue.text: Mexican being too lax? Ultimately, Miguel prepared…

indicators.note: prepared means made ready, as a dish is, so the gathered letters are reworked
ultimately points to the final letter of the word Miguel

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a Mexican is too relaxed, and the answer is that Miguel is ready after all.
explanation.walkthrough: TOOLAX plus L, the last letter of Miguel ('Ultimately'), are 'prepared' into the answer. The ellipsis leads into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: This salamander lives only in lakes near Mexico City, so it is a creature native to Mexico.

clue.text: One who hunted duck moving east by the edges of Colorado river

parts.words: One who hunted duck moving east
parts.note: ORION, the hunter of Greek myth, with its second O (a duck is a zero score) moved to the end

indicators.note: in an across entry east is the right-hand end, so the O shifts there
the edges of a word are its outer letters

parts.note: outer letters of Colorado

explanation.surface: A duck hunter heading east along the Colorado river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colorado river' is a real river, which hides that only 'river' is the definition; a duck in cricket is a score of zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one of South America's great waterways, flowing through Venezuela to the Atlantic.

clue.text: …about eight tacos, almost gone before the end of meal

indicators.note: before places the rearranged letters ahead of the final piece
gone in the sense of gone wrong or off, so the remaining letters are rearranged
almost means not quite all, so the last letter of tacos is dropped
the end of points to the last letter of the word meal

parts.note: the word whose final letter is taken

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, about eight tacos are almost all eaten before the meal is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims TACOS to TACO, which 'gone' rearranges as OCTA; it comes 'before' L, 'the end of' meal.
explanation.definitionFit: An octal number system counts in base eight, so the word means relating to or based on eight.

clue.text: Antelope smells one charging another

indicators.note: to charge a gun is to load it, so one piece is loaded into another

parts.note: another smell, a strong stink, which takes in the first
one of the smells: body odour, the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: An antelope sniffs out one animal attacking another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smells' is a verb in the surface but a plural noun in the wordplay: one smell is loaded into another.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a small grey South African antelope, also spelt rhebok, which gave a trainer brand its name.

clue.text: Went up and down a lot

indicators.note: in a down entry, a word written going up reads backwards

parts.note: went = urinated, a slangy sense

explanation.surface: Something that rose and fell a great deal, like a yo-yo or a share price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went up and down' looks like one phrase; split it into 'went up', the wordplay, and 'down a lot', the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that reaches far below the surface, like a well or ocean trench, extends a long way downward.

clue.text: Clown turned to identify ringmaster's number two

indicators.note: the whole string is turned round so it reads the other way

parts.note: to as printed
to ID someone is to identify them

indicators.note: the ringmaster's number two is his second in line, here the second letter of the word

parts.note: second letter of ringmaster

explanation.surface: A circus clown asked to pick out the ringmaster's deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: All three pieces are assembled first and the whole lot is turned round; 'number two' reads as a deputy, but means the second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in its insulting sense: someone who acts the fool is a buffoon or a complete fool.

clue.text: Call hot Brazilian footballer back during match

indicators.note: these pieces are written back to front
they sit during, that is inside, another word

parts.note: colours that match tone in; it splits T…ONE round the rest
Pelé, the Brazilian football great
h = hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Ringing a hot Brazilian striker to bring him back mid-match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' is a verb, to tone in with, not a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to ring someone up on the phone.

clue.text: Upset, I duel, having lost the heart of Judy Garland

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of the fodder are thrown into a new order
having lost means the letters named next are taken out of the fodder pool
the heart is the middle, so the two central letters of Judy are taken

parts.note: the name whose middle letters are removed

explanation.surface: An upset fighter in a duel loses heart, which recalls the singer Judy Garland.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite: I DUEL 'having lost' UD, 'the heart of' Judy, leaves IEL, and 'Upset' rearranges it. 'Judy Garland' reads as one name, but Garland is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This Hawaiian flower wreath is worn round the neck, so it is a kind of floral garland.

clue.text: Reveal new singer for Eternal

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the letters of reveal are given a different arrangement

parts.note: Sting is the stage name of the English singer Gordon Sumner

explanation.surface: A music headline: a fresh singer is unveiled for the girl group Eternal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges REVEAL as EVERLA, followed by STING. Eternal was a 1990s British girl group, which is the surface misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lasting for ever, without end, is eternal in the plain sense of the word.

clue.text: Cheek or other facial feature

definitions.meaning: impudent talk, as in 'less of your ___'

explanation.surface: Naming bits of the face: the cheek or some other feature.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheek looks like the facial feature, but it means insolence; the rest of the clue is the second, literal definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: insolent backchat, as in 'less of your lip', and the fleshy rim of the mouth.
